svg.title: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2: serializing the same server-to-client response
svg.desc: Educational technical infographic comparing only server-to-client response serialization. The GET /health request is explicitly labeled context only and its serialization is not shown. The HTTP/1.1 response uses textual status and header lines; the HTTP/2 response uses binary frames and HPACK fields, with short bit splits beside their actual use. Both deliver identical application JSON body bytes, using health rather than status as the JSON key. HTTP status 200 reports protocol success; the separate health field is application data and is not defined or reused by HPACK. A response-table continuation shows examples from the 61 predefined entries with separate header-name and stored-value columns, the first learned full header at number 62, and its later one-byte reference. Request and response compression tables are separate. A prominent top legend separately explains text and value colors, every box fill and border style, notation, decoded-response arrows, header-reuse arrows, and the dashed optional-field outline.
svg.text: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2: one server response
Two HTTP versions carry the same response status, media type and JSON body.

g.text: JSON body and body byte counts
Hex bytes; byte counts are decimal
Orange box: HPACK fields and header learning / reuse
Purple box: frame headers and HTTP separators
Green box: JSON body or decoded application response
White / pale gray: context, raw text and byte totals
White + orange border: header bytes, table or grouping

svg.text: REQUEST CONTEXT ONLY · Client → Server: GET /health (no request body)
HTTP status 200: the HTTP request succeeded; this code does not describe the JSON body.
JSON body {"health":"ok"}: application data reporting health; HTTP does not define the health field.
HPACK compresses headers only; body bytes are sent separately in both HTTP versions.
Text status line + text fields + delimited body
Binary frame envelopes + HPACK field blocks

text.tspan: Empty line ends the header section

svg.text: APPLICATION JSON BODY · 15 BYTES · NO TRAILING NEWLINE
1 Client parses the response status line and fields.
3 Client delivers the 15 body bytes to its application.
DERIVED SIZE OF THE ILLUSTRATED MESSAGE
HTTP/1.1 bodies can also carry binary files.
HPACK: TWO RESPONSE FIELDS IN 19 BYTES
Name #31 = content-type; supply the value application/json
APPLICATION JSON BODY: DATA FRAME · STREAM 1
Optional content-length is omitted; END_STREAM ends the message.
DERIVED SIZE OF THE ILLUSTRATED MESSAGE
This value is 16 bytes; other content-type values can be longer or shorter.
CLIENT DECODES THE SAME SERVER RESPONSE
How this response teaches a header that a later response can reuse
Server response encoder ↔ client response decoder: matching tables on one connection. Request tables are separate.
The store instruction is already in 0x5F.
Server stores the full header while encoding;
No learned-entry number is sent here.
HPACK reserves #1–#61 for its predefined table.
Only selected predefined entries are shown.
The learned table was empty; both ends add #62.
3 LATER RESPONSE: REUSE THE FULL HEADER
Client restores the name AND value.
No application/json value bytes are resent.
Literal = actual value bytes. Table reference = the number identifying a known header.
Assume an empty response table at the start, enough capacity, no other insertions or evictions, and Huffman encoding off.
Length, type, flags and stream ID
make boundaries explicit and allow interleaving.
HPACK replaces known headers with lookups.
New values are sent once, then can be reused.
UTF-8 stays UTF-8. Binary stays binary.
Framing does not reserialize the body.
Scope: both columns show server → client response bytes only. Other fields, request bytes, connection setup, TCP and TLS are omitted.
Sizes are derived for the shown encoding only, not a performance benchmark. Codes are hexadecimal; byte counts are decimal. Dashed outline denotes optional metadata.
